quote: the seven major principles and sixty-two specific techniques that were most likely to prove needful in the Ritual Of Changing One’s Mind
content: The fiction models the method the book has been teaching, and the model is a man alone in a white room. Everything the annotations to this book have found about the reliability of self-correction points the other way: the bias blind spot leaves people unable to detect their own motivated reasoning, awareness-based debiasing has little effect, individual reasoning is weak at self-criticism and strong at evaluating others' arguments, and the procedures with a measured record, adversarial collaboration, red teams, structured decomposition, consider-the-opposite, pre-mortems, are all social or mechanical. The sequence's own favored account of reasoning, Mercier and Sperber's, predicts that a solitary ritual is the setting in which the sixty-two techniques would be least effective. Jeffreyssai's two changes of mind in seven attempts are a base rate the author invented, and no student of the actual sequence has been measured against it. The story is a lovely picture of what the book hoped it had built. The room it should have drawn has two people in it, one of them hostile.
